text.en: Did you know… your body is about 60% water?
text.pcm: You sabi say… your body na about 60% water?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé… ara rẹ̀ jẹ́ nípa 60% omi?

cards.picture: Photo-realistic image of a clear glass of water on a neutral table with soft lighting, no labels or text.

text.en: Most of your cells are filled with water, letting chemical reactions happen and nutrients move around.
text.pcm: Most of your cells full wit water, so chemical reaction fit happen and nutrients fit waka.
text.yo: Ọ̀pọ̀ jùlọ àwọn sẹẹli rẹ̀ kún fún omi, tó ń jẹ́ kí ìbáṣepọ̀ kemika ṣẹlẹ̀ àti kí ìjẹ́un rìn kiri.

cards.picture: High-resolution photomicrograph-style image of many animal cells (cytoplasm visible) in soft colors, no labels or scale bar.

text.en: Water helps blood carry oxygen and keeps your body temperature steady during heat or exercise.
text.pcm: Water dey help blood carry oxygen and e dey steady your body temperature for heat or exercise.
text.yo: Omi ń ràn ẹjẹ́ lọ́wọ́ láti gbe òksíjìn, ó sì máa ń pa ìgbóná ara rẹ̀ mọ́ nígbà ìgbóná tàbí ìmúṣiṣẹ́.

cards.picture: Photo-realistic image of red blood cells in a plasma-like fluid (scientific-style close-up), no labels or text.

text.en: Even a small loss—about 2% of body water—can lower mood, energy and the ability to concentrate.
text.pcm: Even small loss — about 2% body water — fit make mood, energy and concentration drop.
text.yo: Ọ̀pọ̀ kekere kan—nípa 2% ti omi ara—lẹ̀ lè dín ìmọ̀lára, agbára àti ìmúlò ìkópọ̀kàn wọ̀nù.

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a wilted plant leaf beside a fresh green leaf on the same stem, showing visible droop vs. turgor, no text.

text.en: Takeaway: sip water through the day—your 60% needs it to think, move and feel good.
text.pcm: Wetin to sabi: sip water all day — your 60% need am to think, move and feel fine.
text.yo: Kó o rántí: mu omi lẹ́ẹ̀kọ̀ọ̀kan ní gbogbo ọjọ́—60% rẹ̀ nílò rẹ̀ láti rò, láti rìn àti láti máa dà bí ẹni pé ó dáa.

cards.picture: Photo-realistic image of a reusable water bottle half full on a school desk with a notebook blurred in the background, no people or text.

text.en: Did you know… more than 99% of your mitochondria come from your mother?
text.pcm: You sabi say… more than 99% of your mitochondria na from your mama?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé… ju 99% ti mitochondria rẹ̀ wá láti ọwọ́ ìyá rẹ?

cards.picture: photo-real microscopic image of a human egg cell surrounded by many tiny sperm cells, no text or labels

text.en: How: after fertilization, the egg's mitochondria stay and the sperm's are usually removed or destroyed.
text.pcm: How: after fertilization, egg mitochondria stay; sperm mitochondria normally dey removed or dem destroy am.
text.yo: Bá a ṣe rí: lẹ́yìn ìfẹ́mọra, mitochondria tó wà nínú ẹyin máa yọ, mitochondria ọkọ̀ bàjẹ́ tàbí a máa pa wọ́n run.

cards.picture: photo of a lab scientist's gloved hands holding a clear petri dish with cells (no faces, no labels)

text.en: Mitochondria carry their own DNA — the human mitochondrial genome has 37 genes.
text.pcm: Mitochondria get dia own DNA — human mitochondrial genome get 37 genes.
text.yo: Mitochondria ní DNA tirẹ̀—genomu mitochondria ènìyàn ní 37 gíìnsì.

cards.picture: high-resolution electron-microscope style image of mitochondria inside a cell, showing the organelles' shapes, no labels

text.en: Think of it like inheriting the battery pack (the egg's mitochondria) rather than a tiny spare from the sperm.
text.pcm: Think am like you inherit the battery pack (egg mitochondria) no be small spare from the sperm.
text.yo: Rò ó bí ìgba mimuéru ẹyọkan tí o jogún (bákannáa ní fún ẹyin) dítí kó tó jẹ́ ìpamọ́ kékeré láti ìbọ̀kùn sperm.

cards.picture: photo of several AA batteries on a wooden table with one battery clearly separated, no people or text

text.en: Takeaway: mitochondrial disorders and some ancestry tests trace your mother's line — that's why maternal inheritance matters.
text.pcm: Wetin to sabi: mitochondrial wahala and some ancestry tests dey trace your mama side — na why maternal inheritance matter.
text.yo: Kó o rántí: àrùn mitochondria àti díẹ̀ nínú ìdánwò ìran lè tọ́pa ìtẹ́sí ìyá rẹ—ìdí ni tí ìjòkòkòrò ìyá fi ṣe pàtàkì.

cards.picture: photo of a simple family-tree sketch on paper laid on a table, photo frames removed or blank, no people or labels

text.en: Did you know plants split water to make the oxygen we breathe?
text.pcm: You sabi say plants dey split water make the oxygen wey we dey breathe?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé àwọn ọ̀gbìn fọ omi sílẹ̀ kí wọ́n lè ṣe òksíjìn tí a ń mí?

cards.picture: Close-up photo of bright green leaves with sunlight streaming through the leaf surface, no people or labels.

text.en: Inside chloroplasts, light energy splits H2O into oxygen, protons and electrons.
text.pcm: Inside chloroplasts, light energy dey split H2O into oxygen, protons and electrons.
text.yo: Nínú chloroplasts, ìmọ́lẹ̀ yọ H2O sílẹ̀ sí òksíjìn, proton àti ẹlẹ́ktrọnu.

cards.picture: Photoreal microscopic image of chloroplasts inside plant cells, showing green oval structures, no labels.

text.en: Plants use the electrons to build sugars (their food); oxygen is left as a waste product.
text.pcm: Plants dey use the electrons make sugars (their food); oxygen remain as waste.
text.yo: Àwọn ọ̀gbìn lo ẹlẹ́ktrọnu wọ̀nyí láti kọ suga (ounjẹ wọn); òksíjìn sì kù gẹ́gẹ́ bí ìdọ̀tí.

cards.picture: Photo of a healthy green leaf on a plant, with visible vein structure and water droplets, no people.

text.en: Think of sunlight powering a factory that breaks water for materials, with oxygen as the factory’s 'exhaust'.
text.pcm: Think of sunlight dey power factory wey break water for materials, oxygen na the factory 'exhaust'.
text.yo: Rò ó bí oorun tí ń ṣiṣẹ́ agbára fáktòrì kan tó n fọ omi kí ó lè rí ohun èlò, tí òksíjìn jẹ́ 'èéfìn' fáktòrì náà.

cards.picture: Photo-real image of a sunlit industrial silhouette or solar-powered plant at sunrise, no people or signage.

text.en: Over about 2.4 billion years, microbes and plants raised Earth's air to about 21% oxygen — the air you breathe.
text.pcm: Over about 2.4 billion years, microbes and plants raise Earth's air to about 21% oxygen — the air wey you dey breathe.
text.yo: Ní bíi 2.4 bílíọ̀nù ọdún, àwon maikíróòbu ati àwọn ọ̀gbìn gbe afẹ́fẹ́ Ilẹ̀-ayé sí 21% òksíjìn—afẹ́fẹ́ tí o ń mí.

cards.picture: High-resolution photo of Earth from space showing the blue atmosphere and limb glow, no text or labels.

text.en: Did you know trees share food and messages through underground fungal networks?
text.pcm: You sabi say trees dey share food and messages through underground fungal networks?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé igi ń pín oúnjẹ àti ìfiránṣẹ́ lẹ́nu-ọ̀nà pẹ̀lú nẹ́tìwọ́ọ̀kì amu-fungi lábẹ́ ilẹ̀?

cards.picture: Photo-real close-up of a mixed forest floor showing tree roots, leaf litter, and soil layers, with soft sunlight filtering through trees (no people).

text.en: Fungi form mycorrhizal links that connect roots, moving sugars, water and nutrients between plants.
text.pcm: Fungi form mycorrhizal link wey connect roots, dey move sugars, water and nutrients between plants.
text.yo: Fungi ń dá ìjápọ̀ mycorrhizal tí ń so gbongbo pọ̀, tí ń ràn sugars, omi àti ohun ìní-nú ilẹ̀ lọ́wọ́ láàárin ọ̀gbìn.

cards.picture: Scientific photo-real image of a soil cross-section showing plant roots entwined with fine white fungal threads (hyphae), high detail, no labels.

text.en: Mature trees can send food to seedlings and pass chemical warnings when pests attack via these fungal routes.
text.pcm: Big trees fit send food to seedlings and warn others say pests don attack through these fungal way.
text.yo: Àwọn igi tí ti dàgbà lè rán oúnjẹ fún àwọn ìkókó, wọ́n sì lè fi ìkìlọ̀ kemika ránṣẹ́ nígbà tí ẹranko àrùn bá kọlu nípasẹ̀ àwọn ipa fungi wọ̀nyí.

cards.picture: Photo-real image of a healthy young sapling growing near a large tree in a forest, emphasizing proximity and shared ground, no people.

text.en: Scientists call this the “wood wide web” — like an underground internet where trees exchange signals and supplies.
text.pcm: Scientists dey call am “wood wide web” — like underground internet where trees dey exchange signals and supplies.
text.yo: Àwọn onímọ̀ sọ pé èyí jẹ́ “wood wide web” — bí intánẹ́tì abẹ́lẹ̀ ilẹ̀ tí igi fi ń pọ̀ mọ́ra kí wọ́n lè pín àlàyé àti ohun èlò.

cards.picture: Photo-real image of tree trunks spaced in a grove with visible rays of light; foreground shows moss and fungus on the ground, evoking connection, no people.

text.en: Takeaway: forests aren’t solitary — over 90% of land plants link with fungi to share resources and survive together.
text.pcm: Wetin to sabi: forests no dey lone — over 90% of land plants dey link with fungi to share resources and survive together.
text.yo: Kó o rántí: igbó kì í ṣe aláìmọ̀kan—ju 90% ti àwọn ọgbìn ilẹ̀ ni ìbáṣepọ̀ pẹ̀lú fungi láti pín ohun ìní àti láti yára ye papọ̀.

cards.picture: Wide, photo-real panorama of a dense mixed forest canopy from the ground looking up, showing many interconnected trees and branches, no people.

text.en: Did you know… identical twins do NOT have identical fingerprints?
text.pcm: You sabi say… identical twins no get identical fingerprints?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé… ìbejì tó jọ ara náà KÒ ní àmì ọwọ́ (fingerprints) tó dà bí ara wọn?

cards.picture: Close-up macro photo of two inked fingertips side by side showing different swirl patterns, no hands or faces visible.

text.en: Fingerprints start forming in the womb around 10–17 weeks of pregnancy.
text.pcm: Fingerprints start form for womb around 10–17 weeks of pregnancy.
text.yo: Àmì ọwọ́ bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í dà ní inú oyun ní ìbẹ̀rẹ̀ ọ̀sẹ̀ 10–17 ti oyun.

cards.picture: Photo-real scientific image of a developing fetal hand (mid-gestation) rendered in soft medical lighting, no identifiable features.

text.en: Tiny differences in blood flow and finger position shape the ridges as skin grows.
text.pcm: Small difference for blood flow and finger position shape the ridges as skin dey grow.
text.yo: Ìyàtọ̀ kékèké nínú ìṣàn ẹjẹ àti ìpo ìka ṣe ìpinnu bí àwọn igbi ṣe máa dà bí ara wọn bí awọ ara ṣe ń dàgbà.

cards.picture: High-resolution microscope photo of skin ridge patterns developing on a small fingertip, showing tiny textured ridges.

text.en: Think of it like two leaves from the same tree: similar but each has its own veins and edges.
text.pcm: Think am like two leaves from same tree: similar but each get im own veins and edges.
text.yo: Rò ó bí ewé méjì tó wá láti igi kan: wọ́n jọ síra sugbon ọkọọkan ní ìtàn-odi àti ọ̀nà ara rẹ̀.

cards.picture: Clear close-up photo of two different leaves on a plain background highlighting distinct vein patterns, no people.

text.en: Takeaway: fingerprints are unique—even for identical twins—so they’re great for identifying people.
text.pcm: Wetin to sabi: fingerprints unique — even identical twins get different ones — so dem good for ID.
text.yo: Kó o rántí: àmì ọwọ́ jẹ́ aláìṣeṣe—paapaa fún ìbejì tó jọ—nítorí náà wọ́n wúlò gan-an fún idanimọ̀.

cards.picture: Photo of a fingerprint on a glass surface under soft light, crisp ridge detail, no text or labels.

text.en: Did you know your bones are alive and rebuild themselves all the time?
text.pcm: You sabi say your bones dey alive and dem dey rebuild themselves all the time?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé egungun rẹ̀ jẹ́ alààyè tí ó ń tún ara rẹ̀ ṣe nígbà gbogbo?

cards.picture: Photo-real close-up of a clean human femur cross-section (bone texture visible), no people, clinical lighting

text.en: This is called remodeling: osteoclasts break down old bone and osteoblasts build new bone.
text.pcm: This one be remodeling: osteoclasts dey break old bone and osteoblasts dey build new bone.
text.yo: Èyí ni a ń pè ní remodeling: osteoclasts máa ba egungun tí kò ṣeé lo run, osteoblasts sì máa kọ egungun tuntun.

cards.picture: Scientific photomicrograph showing bone cells on bone surface (osteoclasts and osteoblasts), labelled appearance but no text, high magnification

text.en: About 10% of your skeleton is replaced every year to keep bones strong and repair tiny damage.
text.pcm: About 10% of your skeleton dey replace every year to keep bone strong and repair small damage.
text.yo: Nípa 10% ti egungun rẹ̀ ni a máa rọ́pò ní gbogbo ọdún láti jẹ́ kí egungun lágbára àti láti tún ìfarapa kékeré ṣe.

cards.picture: Photo of a pile of small, interlocking bones (e.g., vertebrae model) on a neutral background, no people

text.en: Think of bones like a road crew: crews remove potholes then pour fresh concrete to keep the road safe.
text.pcm: Think of bones like road crew: dem remove potholes then pour fresh concrete make road safe.
text.yo: Rò egungun bí ẹgbẹ́ ìtọju ọ̀nà: wọ́n máa yọ́ ibòkùn run kí wọ́n tó fi kọnkírítì tuntun rọ́pò.

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a road crew repairing pavement with asphalt machines, no visible faces or recognisable people

text.en: Takeaway: support remodeling — calcium ~1300 mg/day (teens), vitamin D ~600 IU/day, and stay active.
text.pcm: Wetin to sabi: support remodeling — calcium ~1300 mg/day (teens), vitamin D ~600 IU/day, and dey active.
text.yo: Kó o rántí: ṣèrànwọ́ fun ìtúnṣe—calcium ~1300 mg/day (àwọn ọdọ), vitamin D ~600 IU/day, kí o sì máa ṣiṣẹ́-ara.

cards.picture: Photo of a balanced selection of calcium-rich foods (milk, yogurt, leafy greens) and a vitamin D supplement bottle on a kitchen counter, no people

text.en: Did you know your stomach makes acid strong enough to dissolve some metals in lab tests?
text.pcm: You sabi say your belle dey make acid wey fit dissolve some metals for lab?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé ìkùn rẹ ń ṣe ọ̀tá àcid tó lagbara tó lè tú àwọn irin kan ní ìdánwò yàrá?

cards.picture: photo-real close-up of a glass beaker with bubbling clear liquid in a lab setting, metal spatula tip submerged, no labels

text.en: Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid (HCl) with pH around 1.5–3.5 — very acidic for digesting food and killing microbes.
text.pcm: Your belle dey produce hydrochloric acid (HCl) wey get pH around 1.5–3.5 — very acidic to chop food and kill germs.
text.yo: Ìkùn rẹ ń ṣe hydrochoric acid (HCl) pH rẹ̀ jẹ́ ní àárín 1.5–3.5 — ó ṣé gan-an fún ìjẹ́jẹ̀un àti pípárẹ́ arágbá òòrùn.

cards.picture: photo-real scientific image of a lab flask with a probe measuring acidic solution, neutral background, no labels

text.en: That acid helps break proteins and activates the enzyme pepsin to digest food and reduce bacteria in the gut.
text.pcm: That acid dey help tear protein and activDate enzyme pepsin to digest food and cut down bacteria for gut.
text.yo: Àcid yìí ràn lọ́wọ́ láti fọ́ amíni-òtẹ̀ (proteins) àti láti βìdá ènzyme pepsin kí ó lè jẹ́ kíkún ounjẹ àti dín kokoro arun ku ní ìyẹ̀fun inú.

cards.picture: photo-real endoscopic-style image of stomach lining showing glossy mucus-covered folds, no people

text.en: It’s stronger than lemon juice (pH ~2). In lab tests strong acid can slowly dissolve some metals like iron, but not resistant metals like gold.
text.pcm: E stronger pass lemon juice (pH ~2). For lab, strong acid fit slowly dissolve some metals like iron, but no fit for metals wey dey resistant like gold.
text.yo: Ó ju omi osan lọ ní ìmọ́lẹ̀ (pH ~2). Ní ìdánwò yàrá, ọ̀tá àcid tó lágbára lè tú àwọn irin bí ìrìn díẹ̀, ṣùgbọ́n kì í tú irin tí kò rọ́jú bí wúrà.

cards.picture: photo-real still life of a sliced lemon beside a rusty nail and a shiny gold coin on a neutral surface, no labels

text.en: Takeaway: stomach acid is chemically powerful but your body protects the stomach with mucus—don’t test it by swallowing metal!
text.pcm: Takeaway: stomach acid get power chemically but your body dey protect stomach with mucus—no try am by swallow metal!
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀: àcid ìkùn ló ní agbára kemika ṣùgbọ́n ara rẹ̀ ń dáàbò bo ìkùn pẹ̀lú mucus — má ṣe dán án wò nípasẹ̀ títẹ irin sí ẹnu!

cards.picture: photo-real close-up of stomach lining under light showing a protective mucus layer, medical-scientific look, no people

text.en: Did you know? Your bones store calcium and send it into your blood to keep levels steady.
text.pcm: You sabi? Your bones dey store calcium and dem for release am enter blood make levels steady.
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé egungun rẹ ń tọju kalisiọ̀mù, ó sì lè fi sí ẹ́jẹ̀ kí iye rẹ̀ má bàjẹ́?

cards.picture: Photo-real image of a clean anatomical skeleton model standing against a neutral background, no people or text.

text.en: About 99% of your body's calcium is in your bones and teeth; roughly 1% is in blood and cells.
text.pcm: About 99% of your body's calcium dey for your bones and teeth; about 1% dey for blood and cells.
text.yo: Ní ìwọ̀n: 99% kalisiọ̀mù ara rẹ wà ninu egungun àti eyín; ìdíẹ̀ 1% wà ninu ẹ́jẹ̀ àti sẹ́lù.

cards.picture: Close-up photo of a dental model showing teeth and jawbone next to a specimen bone on a lab bench, no people or labels.

text.en: If blood calcium drops, parathyroid hormone tells bone cells to release calcium; if high, they store it.
text.pcm: If blood calcium fall, parathyroid hormone go tell bone cells to release calcium; if e high, dem go store am.
text.yo: Tí kalisiọ̀mù ẹjẹ bá ṣubú, homoni parathyroid máa sọ fún sẹ́lù egungun kí wọ́n ṣí ìkànsí kalisiọ̀mù; tí ó bá ga, wọ́n máa fipamọ́ rẹ̀.

cards.picture: Microscopic photo-real image of bone tissue with visible osteocytes in their lacunae, no labels or annotations.

text.en: Think of bones like a bank: they withdraw or deposit calcium so blood stays about 9–10 mg/dL.
text.pcm: Think of bones like bank: dem dey withdraw or deposit calcium so blood go remain about 9–10 mg/dL.
text.yo: Rò egungun bí ilé-ifowópamọ́: wọ́n ń yọ tàbí fi kalisiọ̀mù pamọ́ kí ẹjẹ lè wà ní ìwọ̀n tó tó — nípa 9–10 mg/dL.

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a piggy bank beside a glass of milk and a plate with cheese and broccoli on a table, no people or text.

text.en: Takeaway: strong bones are a mineral reserve. Eat calcium-rich foods and get vitamin D to keep that reserve healthy.
text.pcm: Takeaway: strong bones be mineral reserve. Chop calcium-rich food and get vitamin D to keep that reserve healthy.
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀: egungun tó lágbára jẹ́ ìpamọ́ oníminera. jẹun onjẹ tó kún fún kalisiọ̀mù kí o sì gba vitamin D láti pa àpamọ́ náà mọ́ra.

cards.picture: Photo of a bright, natural scene showing a bowl of yogurt, almonds, leafy greens and sunlight on a windowsill, no people or labels.

text.en: Did you know your gut holds about 40 trillion microbes that help digest food and train your immune system?
text.pcm: You sabi say your gut carry about 40 trillion microbes wey dey help digest food and train your immune system?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé iní-ara (gut) rẹ kún fún bí ìlẹ̀ẹ̀bá-trilion 40 (40 trillion) àwọn kokoro tí ń ràn ọ́ lọ́wọ́ láti tú ounjẹ àti kọ́ ààrẹ-ara?

cards.picture: Close-up photo of the inside of a laboratory incubator with Petri dishes and test tubes arranged neatly, soft lighting, no labels or people.

text.en: How they help: gut microbes break down complex foods your body can’t—like fibers—into smaller, usable nutrients.
text.pcm: How dem dey help: gut microbes dey break down complex foods wey body no fit — like fibers — into smaller, usable nutrients.
text.yo: Bí wọ́n ṣe ràn lọ́wọ́: àwọn kokoro inú iní-ara ń fọ àwọn onísọ̀ọkọ tí ara rẹ̀ kò lè, bí fibers, sí ìkan kékèké tí ara lè lò.

cards.picture: Macro photo of a handful of mixed high-fiber foods (whole grains, beans, fruits, vegetables) on a wooden table, natural light, no people or packaging.

text.en: They also make helpful compounds, like short-chain fatty acids, that feed your gut cells and support health.
text.pcm: Dem still dey make helpful compounds, like short-chain fatty acids, wey dey feed your gut cells and support health.
text.yo: Wọ́n tún ń ṣe àwọn ohun amíyẹ̀tọ́ bí àwọn fatty acids kékèké (short-chain fatty acids) tí ń tọ́jú sẹ́lù iní-ara kí o sì ṣe ìlera.

cards.picture: Photo-real scientific image of a high-resolution microscopic view of intestinal tissue (no labels) showing textured folds and cells, realistic coloring.

text.en: Why it matters: microbes teach your immune cells what’s safe and what’s not, lowering chronic inflammation risk.
text.pcm: Why e matter: microbes dey teach your immune cells wetin safe and wetin no be, so e reduce risk of chronic inflammation.
text.yo: Kí nìdí tí ó ṣe pàtàkì: àwọn kokoro kọ́ àwọn sẹ́lù ààrẹ rẹ̀ ohun tí ó ní ṣíṣe àti ohun tí kò ní — èyí dín ewu ìfarapa àìlera tó péye.

cards.picture: Photo of a tidy research workspace showing pipettes and clear lab glassware on a bench, with a blurred background, no people or labels.

text.en: Takeaway: trillions of tiny helpers live in your gut—feed them well with fiber-rich foods to keep you healthy.
text.pcm: Takeaway: trillions of small helpers dey your gut—feed dem well with fiber-rich foods to keep you healthy.
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀: ẹgbẹ̀rún bilionu trilion mẹ́rìnlọ́gọ́rin (40 trillion) iranwọ́ kékeré wà ninu iní-ara rẹ — fún wọn ní oúnjẹ rere pẹ̀lú onjẹ ọlọ́wọ̀ fiber kí ìlera má bàjẹ́.

cards.picture: Warm, inviting photo of a colorful bowl of salad with whole grains and beans on a kitchen counter, natural light, no people or text.

text.en: Did you know muscles always pull and never push?
text.pcm: You sabi? Muscles dey always pull, dem no dey push.
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé iṣan máa fa ṣùgbọ́n kì í tẹ̀?

cards.picture: Photoreal close-up of an anatomical arm model showing detailed muscle fibers and tendons, no labels or text

text.en: A muscle shortens to pull a bone, making a joint move.
text.pcm: Muscle go shortten to pull bone, make joint move.
text.yo: Iṣan máa kùrò kí ó fa egungun, èyí tí yóò mú kí ìjápọ̀ kan rìn.

cards.picture: Photoreal scientific image of an elbow joint model with bone ends and a contracting muscle shown mid-motion, no labels

text.en: There’s another muscle on the other side that pulls it back — they work as antagonistic pairs.
text.pcm: Another muscle for the other side go pull am back — dem dey work as antagonistic pairs.
text.yo: Iṣan mìíràn wà lórí ẹgbẹ̀ kejì tí yóò fa ẹ̀yà náà padà — wọ́n máa ṣiṣẹ́ gẹ́gẹ́ bí ẹgbẹ́ alatako.

cards.picture: Photoreal view of an arm model from the side showing both biceps and triceps muscles on opposite sides, no text

text.en: Like a tug-of-war: biceps curl the forearm up, triceps pull it down — controlled back-and-forth.
text.pcm: Like tug-of-war: biceps dey curl forearm up, triceps dey pull am down — dem dey control back-and-forth.
text.yo: Bí ìdìpò ìja: biceps máa fa ọ̀wọ́ sórí, triceps máa fa ọ̀wọ́ sí abẹ́ — ìṣakoso nínú rírìn padà àti wíwọ̀n.

text.en: Takeaway: paired muscles let you move smoothly and hold posture — muscles always pull, never push.
text.pcm: Takeaway: paired muscles make you move smooth and hold posture — muscles always pull, never push.
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀: ìṣan ìwọ̀n-ìkẹta ń jẹ́ kí ìrìn rẹ dùn ún, kí o sì lè di ìpò — iṣan máa fa lẹ́ẹ̀kansi, kì í tẹ̀.

text.en: Did you know octopuses have three hearts and blue blood?
text.pcm: You sabi octopus get three hearts and blue blood?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé ìkèpẹ̀-omi (octopus) ní ọkàn mẹ́ta àti ẹ̀jẹ̀ buluu?

cards.picture: Close-up photo of an octopus in a rocky reef, tentacles spread and eye visible, natural colors, no people or text.

text.en: Two hearts pump blood to the gills; one heart pumps blood to the rest of the body.
text.pcm: Two hearts dey pump blood go gills; one heart dey pump blood go the rest of body.
text.yo: Mẹ́jì nínú wọn máa tẹ ẹ̀jẹ̀ sí àwọn eefin; ọkàn kan máa tẹ ẹ̀jẹ̀ sí gbogbo ara.

cards.picture: Photo-real scientific dissection image of an octopus showing internal organs (gill area and central body), no labels or text.

text.en: Their blood is blue because it uses copper-rich hemocyanin, not iron-based hemoglobin, to carry oxygen.
text.pcm: Their blood blue because e use copper-rich hemocyanin, not iron-based hemoglobin, to carry oxygen.
text.yo: Ẹ̀jẹ̀ wọn jẹ́ buluu torí ó lo hemocyanin tó kún fún kòpà (copper), kì í ṣe hemoglobin tó ní irin (iron), láti gbé atẹ́gùn.

cards.picture: Microscope-style photo of blue-stained octopus blood/hemocyanin solution, high detail, laboratory setting but no people or labels.

text.en: This system helps in cold, low-oxygen water—two hearts keep gills oxygenated while one keeps the body going.
text.pcm: This system dey help for cold, low-oxygen water—two hearts keep gills oxygenated while one dey keep body going.
text.yo: Ètò yìí ràn wọ́n lọ́wọ́ ní omi tó tutù tàbí ẹni tí atẹ́gùn rẹ̀ kéré — ọkàn mẹ́jì máa jẹ́ kí eefin ní atẹ́gùn nígbà tí ọkàn kan máa tọ́jú ara.

cards.picture: Photo of an octopus in cold, deep-blue seawater among rocks, dim light suggesting deeper, low-oxygen habitat, no people or text.

text.en: Three hearts + copper blood = a clever ocean survival trick you won't find in humans!
text.pcm: Three hearts + copper blood = clever ocean survival trick we no get for humans!
text.yo: Ọkàn mẹ́ta + ẹ̀jẹ̀ kòpà = ọgbọ́n ìgbéyàrá omi tí ìwọ kì yóò rí nínú ènìyàn!

cards.picture: Photo of an octopus perched on a rock, looking alert and curious, clear focus, no people or text.

text.en: Did you know male seahorses get pregnant and carry the babies?
text.pcm: You sabi say male seahorses dey get pregnant and carry babies?
text.yo: Ṣé o mọ̀ pé àwọn ọkùnrin ìkòkò-ẹja (seahorses) ló máa loyún tí ó sì máa bó ọmọ?

cards.picture: Photo-real underwater shot of a single male seahorse in profile, pouch visible, against seagrass background

text.en: How it starts: the female deposits eggs into the male’s brood pouch and he fertilises them there.
text.pcm: How e start: female dey put eggs inside male brood pouch and he dey fertilise dem there.
text.yo: Bí ó ṣe bẹ̀rẹ̀: ìyàwó máa fi ẹyin sínú apò ìtọ́jú ọkùnrin, ó sì jẹ́ kí ọkùnrin náà tún wọn níbẹ̀.

cards.picture: Close-up photo of a pair of seahorses touching; the female’s ovipositor near the male’s pouch (no people, natural reef setting)

text.en: Inside his pouch the male supplies oxygen and nutrients, then carries the embryos for about 2–4 weeks.
text.pcm: Inside his pouch male dey give oxygen and nutrients, then dey carry embryos for about 2–4 weeks.
text.yo: Nínú apò ìtọ́jú rẹ̀, ọkùnrin náà ń pèsè atẹ́gùn àti ohun èlò, ó sì máa gbé àwọn embryos fún bí ọ̀sẹ̀ 2–4.

cards.picture: Detailed scientific-style photo of a swollen male seahorse pouch, showing texture and slight bulge indicating developing young

text.en: Think of it like a built-in incubator: he can release from a few dozen to over 1,000 fully formed baby seahorses.
text.pcm: Think am like built-in incubator: he fit release from few dozen to over 1,000 fully formed baby seahorses.
text.yo: Rò ó bí ìwẹ́ àtọ́jú tó wà lórí ara: ó lè tú láti díẹ̀ sí ọ̀gọ́rùn-ún méjì sí ju 1,000 ọmọ kekere seahorse tí ó ti pé.

cards.picture: Photo-real image of tiny juvenile seahorses (newborns) swimming just released into open water among plankton

text.en: Takeaway: seahorses flip the usual roles — real male pregnancy is one of nature’s coolest surprises.
text.pcm: Takeaway: seahorses turn the usual role — male pregnancy na one of nature’s coolest surprises.
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀: seahorses yí ipa wọ́n padà — ìyọnu ìyẹn: oyún ọkùnrin gan-an jẹ́ ìyanu ìbí-ara nínú iseda.

cards.picture: Vivid underwater scene with an adult seahorse silhouette against sunlit water and swaying seagrass, evoking wonder

text.en: Did you know honeybees “dance” to tell nestmates exactly where food is?
text.pcm: You sabi say honeybees dey “dance” to tell their kontri bees exactly where food dey?
text.yo: Ṣe o mọ̀ pé àwọn agbọńgbẹ́ ìnnàkànmọ́ (honeybees) “ń jó” láti sọ fún àwọn ẹlẹgbẹ́ inú ìtùnú nípò tí oúnjẹ wà gẹ́gẹ́ bí ìtọ́nisọ́nà?

cards.picture: Close-up photo of a honeybee on a honeycomb, body mid-waggle with blurred motion of abdomen, no people

text.en: A forager performs the waggle dance on the comb: the angle of the waggle relative to vertical equals the angle to the sun.
text.pcm: One forager dey do waggle dance for the comb: angle wey e waggle make relative to vertical na the angle to the sun.
text.yo: Olùkójọ oúnjẹ máa ń ṣe ìjó waggle lórí ẹni kọ́mbù: igun ìwàláàyè waggle sí inaro dàbí igun sí oòrùn.

cards.picture: Macro image of a bee on a vertical comb inside a hive, showing the bee’s body aligned at a clear angle to the comb, no labels or people

text.en: The duration of the waggle run encodes distance—longer waggles mean the food source is farther away.
text.pcm: How long the waggle run dey last na how far the food be—longer waggle mean say food dey farther.
text.yo: Ìpẹ̀yà ìgbà waggle ni kó ìjìnlẹ̀ jìnà — waggle tí ó gùn ju túmọ̀ sí pé oúnjẹ wà jìnà síi.

cards.picture: Sharp photo of a single honeybee flapping flight toward a distant patch of brightly colored flowers under a sunny sky, no people

text.en: Think of it as a tiny compass plus map: angle = direction to the sun, waggle length = how far to go.
text.pcm: Think am as small compass plus map: angle = direction to the sun, waggle length = how far you go.
text.yo: Rò ó gẹ́gẹ́ bí kómpás kékeré pẹ̀lú maapu: igun = ìtọ́sọ́nà sí oòrùn, ìgùn waggle = bí jìnà tó wà.

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a paper map and a small brass compass on a wooden table, no people or text

text.en: Tiny dancer, huge teamwork — the waggle dance is a clear example of symbolic animal communication.
text.pcm: Small dancer, big teamwork — waggle dance na clear example say animals fit use signs take communicate.
text.yo: Olùjó kékeré, iṣọkan ńlá — ìjó waggle jẹ́ àpẹẹrẹ kedere ti ìbánisọ̀rọ̀ aami ní àwọn ẹranko.

cards.picture: Inside view of a busy hive with many worker bees on combs, close but no identifiable faces or people

text.en: Did you know some frogs can freeze solid and still survive when they thaw?
text.pcm: You sabi say some frogs fit freeze comot finish and still survive when dem thaw?
text.yo: Ṣe o mọ̀ pé díẹ̀ nínú àwọn ikòkò lè di dídí àti ṣi ṣààyè nígbà tí wọ́n bá tóbọ́?

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a wood frog (Rana sylvatica) sitting on damp leaf litter in a forest, no people.

text.en: Wood frogs can stop breathing and freeze up to 65% of their body water during winter.
text.pcm: Wood frogs fit stop dey breathe and freeze up to 65% of their body water for winter.
text.yo: Àwọn wood frogs lè dá ìmí dúró kí wọ́n sì di tó 65% ti omi ara wọn nígbà ìgbà ọ̀tún.

cards.picture: Photo-real scientific image of a frog curled on snow and ice at the edge of a frozen wetland, close and natural, no people.

text.en: Their liver floods the body with glucose (sugar) that acts like antifreeze, protecting cells from ice damage.
text.pcm: Their liver go pump glucose (sugar) enter body wey act like antifreeze, so cells no go spoil from ice damage.
text.yo: Ìbànújẹ́ wọn ni pé ẹ̀dá ọ̀fun wọn kún fún glúkósì (súgà) tó ń ṣiṣẹ́ bí ìfarapa-ìdènà-dídùn, tó ń bójú tó àwọn sẹ́lì kúrò nínú ìpalára yinyin.

cards.picture: Photo-real microscopic image of crystalline sugar granules (glucose) under magnification, bright and detailed, no labels.

text.en: Think of it like sugar protecting a frozen dessert: ice forms outside cells, while the cells stay safe and intact.
text.pcm: Think am like sugar wey dey protect frozen dessert: ice go form outside cells, while cells remain safe and intact.
text.yo: Rò ó bí súgà tó ń bójú tó onjẹ ìdáná tí a ti jẹ́ kó tutù: yinyin máa ń dá síta sẹ́lì, ṣùgbọ́n sẹ́lì wọ́n wà nípamọ́ àti nípè.

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a scooped frozen dessert (ice cream) with visible sugar crystals, in a natural kitchen-style setting, no people or text.

text.en: When spring warms them, they thaw, start breathing again and hop off—ready for a new season.
text.pcm: When spring warm dem, dem go thaw, begin breathe again and jump comot — ready for new season.
text.yo: Nígbà tí ìgbà oru ó rọ̀ọ̀rùn, wọ́n máa tóbọ́, bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í mi lẹ́ẹ̀kan sì ṣèṣìgàṣí—wọ́n setan fún ìgbà tuntun.

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a wood frog mid-hop at the edge of a thawing pond with fresh spring plants, no people.

text.en: Did you know… bats are the only mammals that truly fly?
text.pcm: You sabi… bats na only mammals wey dey really fly?
text.yo: Ṣe o mọ̀ pé… àwọn bátì (bats) ni ìkan ṣoṣo nínú àwọn ẹranko aláàyè tí ń fo gan-an?

cards.picture: Photo of a bat in midair at dusk with wings fully spread, against a dark sky; no people or text.

text.en: Their wings are a thin skin stretched over very long fingers — basically hands turned into wings.
text.pcm: Their wings na thin skin wey dey stretch over very long fingers — basically hands wey turn wings.
text.yo: Àwọ́n ìwọ̀n òjò wọn jẹ́ àwọ̀n àráfẹ́fẹ́ tinrin tí a fa sí i lórí ìka ọwọ́ gíga—níyẹn bí ọwọ́ ṣe di ìyẹ́.

cards.picture: High-resolution close-up photo of a bat wing spread wide, showing elongated finger bones and thin membrane; clinical, no labels or people.

text.en: Those wings let bats flap to generate lift and thrust, enabling powered flight like birds.
text.pcm: Those wings make bats fit flap to produce lift and thrust, so dem get powered flight like birds.
text.yo: Àwọn ìyẹ́ wọ̀nyí jẹ́ kí bátì lè fọ̀ kí wọ́n sì ṣe ìmúlòtọ́ àti ìfọ̀rọ̀pọ̀, kí wọ́n lè ní ìfojúsùn bíi àwọn ẹyẹ.

cards.picture: Action photo of a bat beating its wings while flying, slight motion blur to show active flapping; no people.

text.en: By contrast, gliders (like flying squirrels) stretch skin to coast but can’t flap to stay aloft.
text.pcm: For difference, gliders (like flying squirrels) just stretch skin to glide but dem no fit flap to remain for air.
text.yo: Ní ìbáṣepọ̀, àwọn alákóbá (gẹ́gẹ́ bí flying squirrels) kan fa awọ̀ ìṣọ̀kan kí wọ́n lè mà lọ ṣùgbọ́n kì í lè fọ̀ láì fọ́n kúrò nílẹ̀.

cards.picture: Photo of a flying squirrel mid-glide between trees, skin stretched like a parachute; natural forest background, no people.

text.en: Takeaway: bats are the only mammals with real, powered flight — nature’s true night pilots.
text.pcm: Takeaway: bats na only mammals wey get true, powered flight — nature own night pilots.
text.yo: Ẹ̀kọ́: bátì ni ìkan ṣoṣo aláàyè tí ó ní ìfojúsùn ìfojúro gidi—awọn olùkọ̀ oko òru ti iseda.

cards.picture: Silhouette photo of a swarm of bats emerging from a cave at sunset, dramatic sky, no people or text.

text.en: Did you know ice floats? Solid water is less dense than liquid water — that’s why ice stays on top!
text.pcm: You sabi say ice dey float? Solid water get lower density pass liquid water — na why ice dey stay for top!
text.yo: Ṣe o mọ̀ pé yinyin máa wà lórí omi? Omi tí ó di dídà jẹ́ kéré jù ní ìwọn ìdíṣítì ju omi tí kò di lọ—ẹ̀yẹn ni kó jẹ́ pé yinyin wà lókè!

cards.picture: Close-up photo of an ice cube floating in a clear glass of water, seen from the side, no text or people.

text.en: How: at 0°C water freezes and the molecules lock into a hexagonal crystalline shape.
text.pcm: How: at 0°C water go freeze and molecules go lock into hexagonal crystal shape.
text.yo: Bá a ṣe ń ṣẹlẹ̀: ní 0°C omi máa di, àwọn molikúlù náà sì pa ara mọ́ nínú irúfanon hexagonal kan.

cards.picture: Macro photomicrograph of hexagonal ice crystals (snowflake-like structure), realistic scientific image without labels.

text.en: Why: that crystal has more open space — ice has density 0.917 g/cm³ vs liquid water’s 1.000 g/cm³ (at 4°C), so ice takes ≈9% more volume.
text.pcm: Why: that crystal get plenty open space — ice get density 0.917 g/cm³ while liquid water get 1.000 g/cm³ (at 4°C), so ice take ≈9% more volume.
text.yo: Ìdí: ìfarapa yẹn ní àyè ṣofo síi — yinyin ní density 0.917 g/cm³ vs omi líkìdù 1.000 g/cm³ (ní 4°C), nítorí náà yinyin máa gba ≈9% ilẹ̀ tó pọ̀ síi.

cards.picture: High-resolution photo of a chunk of ice beside a similar amount of liquid water on a plain surface (no labels, no people).

text.en: Everyday: ice cubes and huge icebergs both float because the frozen form is lighter per volume than the liquid below.
text.pcm: Everyday: ice cubes and big icebergs dey float because frozen form lighter per volume than the liquid under am.
text.yo: Ní wọ́nó lojoojúmọ́: yinyin kùbùkùbù àti àwọn iceberg ń jó lórí omi nítorí fọọ́mù tí a ti tú di jẹ́ fẹ́rẹ́ fẹ́ diẹ̀ síi ju omi ní isalẹ lọ.

cards.picture: Dramatic photo of an iceberg floating in the ocean, showing the above-water tip and calm sea surface, no people or text.

text.en: Takeaway: floating ice insulates liquid water below — that helps lakes and oceans protect life in winter.
text.pcm: Takeaway: floating ice dey insulate the water under — that one dey help lakes and oceans protect life during winter.
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀ pípa: yinyin tí ń jó nípa fífi omi líle lásẹ̀lẹ̀—ẹ̀yí máa ń pa omi inú ọdọ̀ àti okun mọ́ ní ìgbà ìtùtù, tó ń dáàbò bo ìyè alààyè.

cards.picture: Winter pond with clear ice and visible water beneath, with reeds at the edge, no people or text.

text.en: Did you know catalysts speed up chemical reactions but aren’t used up in the process?
text.pcm: You sabi catalysts dey speed chemical reactions but dem no dey finish for the process?
text.yo: Ṣe o mọ̀ pé catalysts ń yara ìbáṣepọ̀ kemika ṣùgbọ́n kì í parun nínú ìlànà náà?

cards.picture: Close-up photo of a bubbling colorful chemical reaction in glass beakers on a lab bench, no people visible.

text.en: They work by giving reactants an easier route — lowering the energy needed to react.
text.pcm: Dem dey work by giving reactants easier route — dem lower the energy wey reactants need to react.
text.yo: Wọ́n máa ṣiṣẹ́ nípa fi ipa rọrùn sílẹ̀ fún àwọn reactants—wíwọ́kàn-énìyàn ìtanràn ìṣedéédé tí ó kéré jù.

cards.picture: Photo-real close-up of fine grey catalyst granules spread on a clean glass surface under soft light.

text.en: Think of a tunnel through a hill: a shorter path gets you there faster than climbing over.

text.yo: Rò ó bí ìkan túnẹ́lì sílẹ̀ lára òkè: ipa ìrìnàjò kékèé kan yóò gba ọ lọ́sẹ̀ ju gígun síi lọ.

cards.picture: Realistic photo of a mountain road with a tunnel entrance cutting through a hill, a car passing through, no people visible.

text.en: Example: a car’s catalytic converter speeds exhaust reactions but the catalyst itself stays unchanged.
text.pcm: Example: car catalytic converter dey speed exhaust reactions but the catalyst itself no change.
text.yo: Àpẹrẹ: catalytic converter ọkọ̀ ayọ́kẹ́lẹ́ ń yara ìbáṣepọ̀ exhaust ṣùgbọ́n catalyst náà kò yípadà.

cards.picture: Photo of an exposed catalytic converter on a plain surface, showing its honeycomb structure, no branding or people.

text.en: Quick takeaway: catalysts speed reactions, remain unchanged, and can be used again and again.
text.pcm: Quick takeaway: catalysts dey speed reactions, dem no dey change, and you fit use dem again and again.
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀ kúkúrú: catalysts ń yara ìbáṣepọ̀, wọ́n wà nípo bíbí, wọ́n sì lè tún lo wọ́n lẹ́ẹ̀mẹ̀ta.

cards.picture: Photo of the same catalyst granules beside three identical clear glass vials on a lab bench, suggesting repeated use, no people visible.

text.en: Did you know? Common salt makes ice melt by lowering water’s freezing point.
text.pcm: You sabi? Common salt dey make ice melt by lowering water’s freezing point.
text.yo: Ṣe o mọ̀ pé? Ṣúgà-ọ̀fẹ́ (common salt) máa mú kí yinyin tóbọ́ nípa fífi ìkìlọ̀ pa ìtọ́jú didi omi sílẹ̀.

cards.picture: Close-up photo of coarse salt crystals scattered on the surface of a sheet of ice, with visible texture and frost, no people.

text.en: Salt dissolves in the thin liquid layer that naturally sits on ice, creating salty water that freezes below 0°C.
text.pcm: Salt dey dissolve for the thin wet layer wey dey on ice, making salty water wey go freeze below 0°C.

cards.picture: Macro photo of a thin water film on an ice surface, showing droplets and slight ripples, no people or labels.

text.en: A sodium chloride solution can freeze as low as −21.1°C at its eutectic mix (about 23.3% salt by weight).
text.pcm: A sodium chloride solution fit freeze as low as −21.1°C at its eutectic mix (about 23.3% salt by weight).
text.yo: Àmí: ojútùú sodium chloride lè di níbi −21.1°C ní àkópọ̀ eutectic rẹ̀ (nípa ìwúwo tó ≈23.3% salt).

cards.picture: Photo-real scientific image of a glass beaker with a clear briny solution and a thermometer beside it showing a cold environment, no people or text.

text.en: Everyday example: road crews salt streets and even old ice-cream makers use salt+ice — the salt melts ice and lets things get colder or clear roads.
text.pcm: Everyday example: road crews dey scatter salt for streets and old ice-cream makers dey use salt+ice — salt dey melt ice make things chill more or make roads clear.
text.yo: Àpẹẹrẹ lojoojúmọ́: àwọn agbẹ́ọ̀nà ọ̀nà máa sáltì ọ̀nà àti bí ẹlẹ́rọ̀ ìdáná ice-cream ṣe ń lò salt+ice—salt ń tóbọ́ yinyin kí ó sì jẹ́ kí ohun kan múra síi tàbí kó àwọn ọ̀nà mọ́.

cards.picture: Photo of a snow-covered road with salt spread across the surface by a spreader truck, seen from a distance; no recognizable people or signage.

text.en: Takeaway: Salt forces ice to melt by lowering its freezing point — effective down to about −21°C; below that, other methods are needed.
text.pcm: Takeaway: Salt force ice to melt by lowering its freezing point — e dey work till about −21°C; under dat, you go need other methods.
text.yo: Ìkìlọ̀: Salt máa fa yinyin tóbọ́ nípa mímu ìtọ́jú didi omi kúrò nípò — o munadoko títí di ≈−21°C; ní isalẹ èyí, a nílò ìmúlò mìíràn.

cards.picture: Close-up photo of a salted sidewalk with melting slushy snow and small puddles, no people or identifiable faces.

text.en: Did you know soap traps greasy dirt by forming tiny spheres called micelles?
text.pcm: You sabi say soap dey trap greasy dirt by forming small spheres wey dem dey call micelles?

cards.picture: Close-up photo of white soap suds with small oily droplets suspended in the foam, no people.

text.pcm: Soap molecule get head wey like water and tail wey like oil.

cards.picture: Macro photo of a soap bar next to clear water with droplets, shot to emphasize surface texture and beads of water, no people.

text.en: They surround oily dirt with tails facing in and heads facing out toward the water.
text.pcm: Dem surround oily dirt so tails dey face inside and heads dey face outside towards water.
